description.narrative: CMI!’s vision is a gender-equal and just world where all women, girls, and non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people enjoy their rights fully and live to their full potential. Our role in bringing about this vision is to support movements to be resilient and leverage their power to create change from local to global and from global to local, thereby engendering systemic and sustainable change at all levels.

In order for feminist civil society movements to be strong and autonomous39 (an ambitious achievement in itself), self-led WHRDs and WROs go through three intermediate steps - resulting in CMI!’s output (see section 4 and Annex 1, our Results Framework). WHRDs and WROs must be: RESOURCED with the knowledge, resources, and skills for impact, including for L&A. COORDINATED to be able to organise together to articulate priorities and take collective action, including amplifying voices through alliances between structurally excluded movements, linking with more mainstream movements where possible. RESILIENT by having resources, networks, strength and holistic security in place to sustain their work including in the face of backlash and closing civic space, build broader support bases, and expand their work.

Our five-year strategic objective is: political actors, societal actors and donors at local, national, regional and global levels take action to recognise, protect and fulfil the human rights of all women, girls, and non-binary, gender non-conforming, trans and intersex people as a result of strong and autonomous feminist movements holding them to account.

MSS held three workshops in three districts on human rights and building the capacity of sex workers to form supportive groups and put pressure on police and security personnel not ot arrest sex workers in hotels and public places.NMS strenthened their partnerships with local government officials an with other sex worker-led organisations like Jagriti Mahila Mahasangh (JMMS) and SWASA Nepal, as well as feminist organisations including Womens Fund Asia, and AWID Forum. Sramajibi Mahila Sangha has been an active and committed member of the All India Network of Sex Workers (AINSW), taking a leading role in influencing national policies and programs that benefit the sex worker community. Sramajibi maintains a strong partnership with Durbar Mahila Samanwaya Committee collaborating on initiatives aimed at advancing the sex workers' rights movement. Furthermore, our collaboration with Komal Gandhar has been instrumental in organizing community events, cultural programs, and public relation initiatives that foster greater social acceptance and support for sex workers. During the reporting period, DMSC successfully developed and strengthened its partnerships with several sex worker-led organizations and networks to advocate for the rights and well-being of sex workers and other marginalized communities. DMSC also collaborated with Komal Gandhar, a socio-cultural society, to organize community events and cultural programs. Collaboration with Sramajibi Mahila Sangha enhanced the collective capacity for advocating sex workers' rights and addressing key challenges. These initiatives aimed to foster social acceptance, reduce stigma, and create platforms for public relations through the arts. In addition to these, DMSC worked with Balaram Dey Street Anandam to advocate for LGBTQI+ rights, ensuring that the needs of intersectional identities within the sex worker community are addressed. DMSC also collaborated with organizations of other marginalized communities. Efforts to uplift the Nachni community in Purulia and support their cultural and socio-economic development also continued, reaffirming DMSC’s commitment to addressing the unique needs of historically marginalized groups. Furthermore, DMSC organized a three-day-long fair in Amlasole to celebrate Sabar Rights Day in the month of December, collaborating with Amlasole Birsa Munda Gram Unnayan Committee and Lagadori Gram Kalyan Committee. These efforts highlighted the importance of community-led initiatives and celebrated the culture and resilience of the Sabar and Munda communities.DMSC built relationshipw with law enforcement in six stations to help change the existing policy to address police-led violence and extortion.
